opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of my favorite questions, because I think it gets at the heart of how we'll scale robotics.

The way I think about it is this: if you train an agent in one simulated world, with one set of physics parameters, one set of textures, one lighting condition, it will overfit to that world. It learns all the quirks and artifacts of that particular simulator. When you put it on a real robot, it breaks, because reality is just slightly different in a thousand small ways.

The trick that works surprisingly well is to stop thinking of simulation as one reality and instead think of it as a million different realities. That's the idea behind domain randomization. You randomize the gravity a bit, the friction, the mass of objects, the motor latencies, the camera angles, the colors, the lighting. If a single neural network can solve the task across a million slightly different simulated worlds, then there's a good chance the real physical world is just the million-and-first. From the agent's point of view, reality is another sample from the distribution, and it generalizes to it without ever having seen it.

We've seen this work in practice. You can train a policy in massively parallel GPU simulation, compressing something like ten years of training experience into a couple of hours of wall-clock time, and then transfer it zero-shot to a real robot hand or a quadruped or a humanoid, with no fine-tuning in the real world. That still feels a bit magical to me every time it works.

That said, simulation isn't the whole story. Classical physics simulators are good at rigid-body dynamics, but they still struggle with deformable objects, fluids, cloth, and the long tail of messy real-world contact. And it's very hard to hand-author the diversity of real environments, like all the kitchens, all the objects, all the clutter.

So I think the future is a data pyramid. At the bottom you have internet-scale data, video and text, which gives you common sense and priors about how the world looks and behaves, but no actions. In the middle you have simulation and increasingly neural simulation, meaning generative world models that can dream up new scenarios and fill in what graphics engines can't. At the top you have real robot data, like teleoperation, which is the highest quality but the most expensive and doesn't scale, because it's bounded by human hours and robot hours.

Generalization from sim to real comes from mixing all three carefully. You use simulation for scale and diversity, internet data for broad priors, and a relatively small amount of real data to ground everything. If you get that recipe right, I think we'll see something like a GPT moment for robotics, where one foundation model can control many different bodies across many different tasks, and the line between simulated training and physical deployment becomes much blurrier than it is today.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it, simulation is really the only path that scales. If you look at what made language models work, it was the internet—trillions of tokens of human-generated data just sitting there. Robotics doesn't have that. There is no internet of robot actions. Every real-world trajectory you collect costs hours of a human operator's time, and even the biggest teleoperation efforts get you maybe hundreds of thousands of episodes. That's nothing compared to what a foundation model needs.

So simulation is how we manufacture the data. And the key insight, the thing that made it click for me, is that you don't try to make one perfect simulation that matches reality. That's a losing game. Instead you make the simulation deliberately diverse—you randomize physics parameters, friction, mass, lighting, textures, camera angles, even the robot's own body dimensions—so that the agent sees ten thousand slightly different worlds. Reality then just becomes one more sample from that distribution. If the policy is robust across all those variations, it doesn't really care that the real world is a little different from any individual sim instance.

We did this with Eureka and the follow-up work, where a robot hand learned to spin a pen or balance a ball, and the training was entirely in GPU-accelerated simulation. With something like Isaac, you can run thousands of environments in parallel, so you compress what would be years of real-world experience into a couple of hours of wall-clock time. That's a ten-thousand-x speedup, and that's what lets you brute-force the diversity.

Now, there are things simulation is genuinely bad at. Deformable objects, fluids, really contact-rich manipulation—the physics engines are still approximations, and the gap shows up there. So the way I see the pipeline now is a kind of hybrid. You use real-world data, even a small amount, to anchor the simulation and to calibrate it. You use generative models—video models, essentially neural simulators—to fill in the long tail of visual diversity that a traditional renderer can't capture. And then you use classical physics sim for the things it's good at, which is massive-scale, cheap, and reasonably faithful rigid-body dynamics.

And the last piece is the foundation model itself. When you have a big model that's been pretrained on language and video, it already has a lot of priors about how the world works—objects don't pass through each other, things fall down. So the policy you train in sim is building on top of that common sense rather than from scratch. That makes the transfer much more forgiving. The model isn't memorizing one simulator, it's learning something closer to the actual structure of the task, and that's what generalizes.

r001.rationale: The candidate says reality becomes “one more sample from that distribution” after training across many randomized simulated worlds, conveying the physical world as another configuration.

r002.rationale: It mentions Eureka and follow-up work trained entirely in simulation, but does not say those agents transferred to the physical world without further fine-tuning.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that the agent can’t just memorize one simulated world. It needs to learn skills that survive changes in the world. If you train a robot to pick up a cup, and the cup always has the same weight, the same surface friction, and the same lighting, it may learn a solution that works beautifully in simulation and fails immediately in reality.

So you vary those things. You expose the agent to many different conditions, so it has to discover what remains useful across them: how to approach an object, establish contact, and adjust when the object moves unexpectedly. In that sense, simulation isn’t just a replica of reality. It’s a way to generate a much broader training experience.

But diversity alone doesn’t guarantee transfer. The simulator can still miss something important, especially around contact, sensing, or timing. So I’d judge generalization by whether the agent can use its learned skills in the physical world and adapt from feedback when its expectations are wrong. The goal is not to predict everything perfectly. It’s to act effectively despite that uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response describes training across varied simulated conditions and applying learned skills in the physical world, but does not frame the physical world as another simulated configuration for an agent that has mastered many configurations.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Eureka, a follow-up study, or transfer to the physical world without further fine-tuning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that an agent shouldn’t learn just one simulated world. It should learn across a distribution of worlds—with different objects, different lighting, different friction, even slightly different physics. Then the physical world becomes another variation of what it has already experienced, rather than something completely unfamiliar.

Imagine training a robot to pick up a cup. If it only succeeds with one cup in one position, it may have memorized the setup. If it succeeds across thousands of shapes, materials, and positions, it has a better chance of learning the underlying skill: how to approach, grasp, and adapt when the object moves.

Of course, simulation always leaves something out. Contact, sensing, and hardware can behave differently in reality. So the goal isn’t necessarily perfect zero-shot transfer. It’s to learn a strong foundation in simulation, then use real-world experience to calibrate and improve it. The real test of generalization is whether the agent can handle those differences and recover when its expectations are wrong.
